channels.name: Online
channels.what: An optional, bounded channel, at your word on 2026-09-23. Off until you turn it on, and one switch turns it fully off again: then none of its reps is offered and none is kept. It is never required for any stage and never the route a stage is met by: its reps are solo or remote, and those move no stage. It is bounded: a browse is fifteen minutes and stops, no more than two of its reps are offered in a week, and it points at meeting in person soon. Nothing about how anyone responds is kept or shown: the never-counted list applies to it in full.

acts.name: Your values and non-negotiables, written down
acts.what: A short private note in three parts, typed by you and rewritten whenever you like: the few true non-negotiables, about direction and conduct rather than traits; the preferences you hold loosely; and the partner you want to be. Written before they are tested. Only you read it.

source.who: Jonason, Garcia, Webster, Li and Fisher
source.what: People weigh dealbreakers more heavily than the qualities they want; knowing yours in advance is supported

parts.name: A few true non-negotiables
parts.prompt: About direction and conduct, not traits. For each one: would you end an otherwise good relationship over it?

parts.name: Preferences, held loosely
parts.prompt: What you would like. Held loosely: what people say they want in a partner barely predicts whom they come to want.

parts.name: The partner you want to be
parts.prompt: How you want to treat them, and what you want to bring.

acts.name: Decide, don’t slide
acts.what: Before each step (becoming exclusive, meeting each other’s families, introducing them to your child, moving in, an engagement), a private note: what you are choosing, and why now, written with your own record in front of you: your values, your recent reflections and your earlier notes.

source.what: People who reported deciding their relationship steps thoughtfully reported more dedication and satisfaction than those who slid into them

acts.name: Introducing them to your child
acts.what: If you are a parent: a decision that is yours alone, made deliberately, with a note before it. The app never schedules an introduction and never recommends one. Almost all of what is known comes from mothers after divorce; little is known about fathers raising a child.

source.what: A clinical review: few evidence-based guidelines exist for when and how a parent shares dating with a child or introduces a partner

considerations.text: How steady the relationship is before your child grows close: children who had grown close to a parent’s partner showed more anxiety and withdrawal when it ended, though breakups had no effect overall.
Keeping your own time with your child: a close bond between parent and child softened the effects of a parent’s dating.
considerations.source: Xiao and colleagues 2022; Anderson and Greene 2011

considerations.text: Whether they want a life that includes a child who is already yours: people who said they would marry someone with children were more likely to.
A friend to your child first, while the parenting decisions stay yours: this went with warmer step-relationships in stepfamily studies.
considerations.source: Ganong and colleagues 1999 and 2019; Sanner and colleagues 2022

considerations.text: Fewer changes in who is part of a young child’s life: changes in early childhood weigh most, though how much is debated.
considerations.source: Cavanagh and Huston 2008; Lee and McLanahan 2015

considerations.text: When, where and what to tell your child: no study answers these; the guidance is expert opinion.

acts.name: A monthly reflection
acts.what: Once a month, if you want: a few lines on a moment you felt understood or appreciated, or didn’t; on how your last disagreement ended; and on your own part, and whether it feels chosen by both of you. Words only, never scored: describe the moment rather than analyse it. Never prompted on a hard day.

source.who: Rogge, Cobb, Lawrence, Johnson and Bradbury
source.what: In a randomised trial of 174 engaged and newly married couples, one guided session of reflecting on the relationship matched two skills courses on breakups three years on, among couples who completed them

parts.name: A moment you felt understood or appreciated, or didn’t
parts.prompt: Describe the moment as it happened.

parts.name: Your last disagreement, and how it ended
parts.prompt: How it ended, not who was right.

parts.name: Your own part, and whether it feels chosen by both of you
parts.prompt: What you brought, and whether you both seem to be choosing this.

acts.name: A monthly private check
acts.what: Once a month, three private questions about your own safety, your own conduct, and any doubt you keep setting aside. A yes to the safety or the conduct question shows the app’s own fixed help, inside this check and nowhere else; a doubt on its own does not. No model writes, softens or decides it, and it is not a general crisis screen.

questions.text: In the last month, has anyone you are dating made you afraid, or tried to control where you go, whom you see or what you spend?
Has anything you did toward them worried you afterwards: a raised voice, pressure, checking up on them?
Is there a doubt about this relationship you keep setting aside?

acts.help: If someone’s behaviour frightens you, or your own worries you, you do not have to sort it out alone. The National Domestic Violence Hotline answers day and night: 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788, or thehotline.org. In danger now, call 911.

source.what: The number and frequency of early warning signs, such as reacting badly to a no, predicted abuse six months later

acts.name: A relationship course, if you want one
acts.what: A suggestion, never a requirement: before an engagement, a relationship-education course together, nine to twenty hours rather than a single evening. Taking one is never needed to move on or to declare a step; not taking one blocks nothing and is never counted, flagged or shown as missing.

source.what: Across 148 evaluations, moderate courses of nine to twenty hours did better than short ones of one to eight

paths.parents: For a parent, in general terms. One study found a mother’s dating after divorce had little direct effect on her children’s adjustment; several changes in who lives in a child’s home go with more behaviour problems, partly because of what came before, and a systematic review found that evidence mixed. When and how to introduce a partner to a child has no tested answer: the guidance is expert opinion. The path never schedules an introduction; that stays yours.

excluded.what: Reading signals to decide who is interested
excluded.why: Flirting is detected poorly, and people afraid of rejection think their own overtures say more than they do: say it plainly instead.
Cute or flippant lines are rated worst, a plain or third-party introduction best, and endorsing pickup tactics tracks hostile sexism.

excluded.what: A type, a checklist or a compatibility score
excluded.why: Ideals barely predict whom people come to desire, and what predicts a good relationship is how it works, not a match of traits.
Persistence after a no is the core of harassment; one ask, and anything other than a yes is final.

excluded.what: Someone you supervise, or who supervises you
excluded.why: Harm around workplace romance concentrates where one partner has power over the other (a framework, not a trial).

excluded.what: Matching algorithms, love languages and divorce prediction
excluded.why: None holds up on the evidence (disputed cards); the path never uses them.

excluded.what: Labelling a partner’s attachment style, or opposites attract
excluded.why: Verdicts on another person are never made here, and actual similarity barely predicts satisfaction either way.

excluded.what: A list of answers to look for, or a tally of warning signs
excluded.why: No study shows that ticking topics or counting signs predicts a good match; the talks are for learning each other’s lives, and no answer is a pass or a fail.
